title: A thousand days
hookLine: day one thousand on the hill: a moment to be glad you came this far

cards: The hill doesn't hand out trophies. There's no holy day on any calendar for this one, just a count of mornings and evenings when you opened this and listened.
Before the story turns toward a very hard year, which it does tomorrow, it's worth stopping on the path, turning around, and looking back down at the first step, far below.
So today there's no battle and no reform campaign. There's the place you started, and the place you're standing.

teach.h: DAY ONE: SEVA, A KITCHEN IN AMRITSAR.
teach.b: First, where you began. Day one on this path was a kitchen in Amritsar that feeds everyone who walks in, for free, and the word was seva, selfless service. Your line that day was one quiet thing for someone.
Day two was Waheguru, the word Sikhs say for God, and the line was simply wow: wonder before the One.

Everything since has been built on those two: Gurus and their hymns, martyrs and builders, soldiers and reformers, and a free kitchen that kept feeding strangers all the way through. Third, the spirit for the road.
Sikhs have a phrase for the mood they hope to carry through good years and terrible ones: chardi kala, rising spirits, an upward-climbing heart. It isn't pretending things are fine.

It's staying turned toward the light when they're not. The Ardas, which you met three days ago in a trench, closes by asking that through Nanak the Name may bring rising spirits, and that by God's will all may be well.
Chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, side by side. Fourth, the next stretch. The story is about to go through the year of Partition, and it won't be easy to hear.

teach.h: NOT A WAY AROUND THE HARD PARTS.
teach.b: Chardi kala is not a way of skipping the hard chapters. It's how Sikhs have walked through them.
A thousand days: not a finish line, but a place to stand for a moment, glad, before the path goes on.

how: Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits, as the outlook to keep in good times and hard ones, and the Ardas said at the close of worship ends by asking for chardi kala and the good of all.

o: the closing hymn sung after the Ardas
a festival held when a long fast comes to an end
rising spirits, a heart that keeps climbing

practice: Go back to where you were when you began this path, the room, the season, what was on your mind, and look at that person kindly, without judging.
Then come back to this room and notice one thing that's different now, however small: a word you know, a habit you kept, a story you could tell someone tonight.
Breathe in on then, breathe out on now, and if you pray, let Waheguru be the word for both.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala, rising spirits, an upward-climbing heart: a long count of ordinary mornings on the path, from seva and Waheguru to here. Today's word.

orig.note: rising spirits; an upward-climbing heart, asked for at the close of the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: a place to stand, glad. You're still on the path. One thousand days, and counting.
